title: Operations with constant-specific bodies

blocks.text: In the page's `MathOperation`, the enum declares `abstract double apply(double a, double b)` and every constant supplies its own body. Two consequences the page points out:

items: Each constant must handle its own edge cases. `DIVIDE` **and** `MODULUS` throw `ArithmeticException("Division by zero")` for a zero divisor (plain `double` arithmetic would quietly give `Infinity` or `NaN`).
A constant with a body is an instance of an anonymous subclass, so its `getClass()` is not the enum. `getDeclaringClass()` is.
`static Optional<MathOperation> fromSymbol(String symbol)`: the constant whose symbol equals `symbol`, or empty.
`static String qualifiedName(Enum<?> constant)`: the simple name of the constant's enum type, a dot, and the constant's name, such as `"MathOperation.ADD"` or `"Precedence.HIGH"`.

blocks.text: A symbol usually arrives from parsed input, so it is not the same `String` object as the constant's symbol.

cases.says: Each constant's own body computes its operation, fromSymbol() finds a constant by its symbol, and qualifiedName() names a plain constant.
Both DIVIDE and MODULUS throw ArithmeticException for a zero divisor, -0.0 and 0 / 0 included, instead of returning Infinity or NaN.
fromSymbol() finds a constant by a symbol built at run time, not written as the same literal.
qualifiedName() of a constant with a body names the enum, although the constant's getClass() is an anonymous subclass.

origin.section: Q3: How do constant-specific method bodies work?

concepts: A constant with a body is an anonymous subclass, so getClass() is not the enum and getDeclaringClass() is.
A constant-specific body overrides an abstract method, so each constant carries its own implementation.
Each constant with its own body must handle its own edge cases, such as a zero divisor.
